readings.c1s2:
apprehensive; not fearful or suspecting.
{{smaller block|Careless of the common danger, and, through a haughty ignorance, ''unapprehensive'' of his own.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., iii.}}}}
'''2.''' Not intelligent; not ready of conception, perception, or understanding.
{{smaller block|Unlerned, ''Unapprehensive'', yet impudent.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., iii.}}}}
'''3.''' Unconscious; not cognizant. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I am not ''unapprehensive'' that I might here indeed . . . have proceeded in another manner.
{{right|''J. Howe'', Works, I. 28.}}}}

'''unapprehensiveness''' (un-ap-rē-hen′siv-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unapprehensive. ''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, iii. 5. (''Davies.'')

'''unapprised''' (un-a̤-prīzd′), ''a.'' Not apprised; not previously informed.
{{smaller block|You are not ''unapprized'' of the influence of this officer with the Indians.
{{right|''Jefferson'', to Gen’l Washington (Works, I. 185).}}}}

'''unapproachable''' (un-a̤-prō′cha̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be approached or approximated; inaccessible; unattainable. ''Hammond'', Works, IV. 613.

'''unapproachableness''' (un-a̤-prō′cha̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unapproachable. ''Hawthorne'', Marble Faun, x.

'''unapproachably''' (un-a̤-prō′cha̤-bli), ''adv.'' So as to be unapproachable. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIII. 554.

'''unapproached''' (un-a̤-prōcht′), ''a.'' Not approached; not to be approached; not approximated.
{{smaller block|<poem>God is light,
And never but in ''unapproached'' light
Dwelt from eternity. ''Milton'', P. L., iii. 4.</poem>}}
readings.c2s3:
monly found: as, ''unarmed'' tibiæ.

'''unarmored, unarmoured''' (un-är′mo̤rd), ''a.'' Not armored; specifically, not plated or sheathed with metal as a defense from projectiles: noting ships of war: as, an ''unarmored'' cruiser.

'''unarrayed''' (un-a̤-rād′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not arrayed; not dressed; unappareled.
{{smaller block|This infant world, yet ''unarray’d'', naked and bare.
{{right|''Dryden'', Indian Emperor, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Not organized; not arranged.

'''unarted†''' (un-är′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''art''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Ignorant of the arts.
{{smaller block|God, who would not have his church and people letterless and ''unarted''.
{{right|''Waterhouse'', Apology for Learning (1653), p. 19.}}}}
'''2.''' Not artificial; plain; simple.
{{smaller block|''Unarted'' meat, kind neighbourhood.
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 99.}}}}

'''unartful''' (un-ärt′fu̇l), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not artful; artless; not having cunning; guileless; frank; genuine.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’m sure ''unartful'' truth lies open
In her mind.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', The Tempest, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' Wanting skill; inartistic. [Rare.]

'''unartfully''' (un-ärt′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Without art; in an unartful manner; artlessly. ''Burke.''

'''unartificial''' (un-är-ti-fish′al), ''a.'' Inartificial; not artificial; not formed by art.
{{smaller block|The coarse ''unartificial'' arrangement of the monarchy.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
Hist. Eng., iii.

'''unartistic''' (un-är-tis′tik), ''a.'' Inartistic. ''Edinburgh Rev.''

'''unascendable''' (un-ạ-sen′dạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being ascended, climbed, or mounted; unscalable.

'''unascended''' (un-ạ-sen′ded), ''a.'' Not having been ascended, as a throne waiting for its king. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>It was for thee yon kingless sphere has long
Swung blind in ''unascended'' majesty.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, xlvi.}}}}

'''unascertainable''' (un-as-ėr-tā′nạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being ascertained; incapable of being certainly known.

'''unascertained''' (un-as-ėr-tānd′), ''a.'' Not reduced to a certainty; not made certain and definite; not certainly known.
{{smaller block|Most of the companies administer charities of large but ''unascertained'' value. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', VI. 225.}}}}

'''unascried†''' (un-as-krīd′), ''a.'' Not descried or seen. ''Hall.''

'''unasked''' (un-ȧskt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not asked; unsolicited.
{{smaller block|<poem>Indeed I thought
That news of ill ''unasked'' would soon be brought.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 310.}}}}
'''2.''' Not sought by entreaty or care. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The bearded corn ensu’d
From earth ''unask’d''.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''unaspective†''' (un-as-pek′tiv), ''a.'' Not having regard to anything; inattentive. ''Feltham'', Resolves, ii. 74.

Not applauding; not cheering or encouraging by or as by applause. {{smaller block|Instead of getting a soft fence against the cold, shadowy, ''unapplausive'' audience of his life, had he only given it a more substantial presence? {{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xx. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''unappliable''' (un-a̤-plī′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Inapplicable. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Best books to a naughty mind are not ''unappliable'' to occasions of evill. {{right|''Milton'', Areopagitica, p. 16.}}}} '''unapplicable''' (un-ap′li-ka̤-bl), ''a.'' Inapplicable. ''Boyle'', Works, II. 485. [Rare.] '''unapplied''' (un-a̤-plīd′), ''a.'' Not specially applied; not put or directed to some special object or purpose. {{smaller block|Men dedicated to a private, free, ''unapplied'' course of life. {{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}}} '''unappreciable''' (un-a̤-prē′shi-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Inappreciable. [Rare.] '''unappreciated''' (un-a̤-prē′shi-ā-ted), ''a.'' Not appreciated. {{smaller|(''a'') Not perceived or detected. (''b'') Not estimated at the true worth; not sufficiently valued.}} '''unappreciative''' (un-a̤-prē′shi-ā-tiv), ''a.'' Inappreciative. ''The Academy'', May 3, 1890, p. 309. '''unapprehended''' (un-ap-rẹ̄-hen′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not apprehended; not taken.—'''2.''' Not understood, perceived, or conceived of. {{smaller block|They of whom God is altogether ''unapprehended'' are but few in number. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 2.}}}} '''unapprehensible''' (un-ap-rē-hen′si-bl), ''a.'' Inapprehensible. ''South'', Sermons, V. v. '''unapprehensive''' (un-ap-rē-hen′siv), ''a.'' '''1.''' '''unapprised''' (un-a̤-prīzd′), ''a.'' ''Hawthorne'', Marble Faun, x. '''unapproachably''' (un-a̤-prō′cha̤-bli), ''adv.'' So as to be unapproachable. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIII. 554. '''unapproached''' (un-a̤-prōcht′), ''a.'' Not approached; not to be approached; not approximated. {{smaller block|God is light, And never but in ''unapproached'' light Dwelt from eternity. ''Milton'', P. L., iii. 4. Those scenes of almost ''unapproached'' pathos which make the climax of his [Dante’s] Purgatorio. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 76.}}}} '''unappropriate''' (un-ạ-prō′pri-āt), ''a.'' '''1.''' Inappropriate. [Rare.]—'''2.''' Not assigned or allotted to any person or persons; unappropriated. ''Warburton.'' '''unappropriate''' (un-ạ-prō′pri-āt), ''v. t.'' To take from the possession or custody of particular individuals; make open or common to the use or possession of all. [Rare.] {{smaller block|''Unappropriating'' and unmonopolising the rewards of learning and industry from the greasy clutch of ignorance. {{right|''Milton.''}}}} '''unappropriated''' (un-ạ-prō′pri-ā-ted), ''a.'' Not appropriated. {{smaller|(''a'') Having no particular application.}} {{smaller block|Ovid could not restrain the luxuriancy of his genius . . . from wandering into an endless variety of flowery and ''unappropriated'' similitudes, and equally applicable to any other person or place. {{right|''T. Warton'', Essay on Pope.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') Not applied or directed to be applied to any other object, as money or funds: as, ''unappropriated'' funds in the treasury. (''c'') Not granted or given to any person, company, or corporation: as, ''unappropriated'' lands. (''d'') Not appropriated by any person: as, an ''unappropriated'' subject for a poem.}} '''unapproved''' (un-ạ-prövd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not approved; not having received approbation. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 118.—'''2†.''' Not justified and con- '''unapt''' (un-apt′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unapt''; < ''un-''1 + ''apt''.] '''1.''' Not apt; not ready or inclined. {{smaller block|I am a soldier, and ''unapt'' to weep. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 133.}} A most merciful man, as ready to forgive as ''unapt'' to take or give an offence. {{right|''Penn'', Rise and Progress of Quakers, v.}}}} '''2.''' Dull; not ready to learn: same as ''inapt'', 2. {{smaller block|Very dull and ''unapt''. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} '''3.''' Unfit; inappropriate; unsuitable; not qualified; not disposed. {{smaller block|Was never man or woman yet bigete That was ''unapt'' to soferen loves hete Celestial, or elles love of kynde. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 978.}} ''Unapt'' I am, not only because of painful study, but also for this short warning. {{right|''Latimer'', 1st Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}} Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, ''Unapt'' to toil and trouble in the world? {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., v. 2. 166.}} No ''unapt'' type of the sluggish and wavering movement of that mind. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xvii.}}}} '''unaptly''' (un-apt′li), ''adv.'' Unfitly; improperly. '''unaptness''' (un-apt′nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unapt, in any sense. '''unaquit†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''1 + ''aquit'', pp. of ''aquit'', ''v.''] Unrequited. {{smaller block|Charitee goth ''unaquit''. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii.}}}} '''unaraced†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''1 + ''araced''.] Same as ''unraced''. '''unargued''' (un-är′gūd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not argued; not debated; also, not argued with; not disputed; not opposed by argument. {{smaller block|My author and disposer, what thou bidd’st
''Unargued'' I obey.{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 636.}}}} '''2†.''' Not censured. ''B. Jonson.'' '''unarm''' (un-ärm′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''unarmen''; < ''un-''2 + ''arm''2.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To strip of armor or arms; disarm. {{smaller block|To ''vnarme'' hym the kyng made in that place.{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5666.}} Sweet Helen, I must woo you To help ''unarm'' our Hector.{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 1. 163.}}}} '''2.''' To render incapable of inflicting injury; make harmless. {{smaller block|Galen would not leave the world too subtle a theory of poisons, ''unarming'' thereby the malice of venomous spirits.{{right|''Sir T. Browne.''}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take off or lay aside one’s arms or armor. {{smaller block|While thei were in ''vn-armynge'', thei saugh comynge the squyer of Elizer and the yoman.{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 555.}} Will ye ''unarm'', and yield yourselves his prisoners?{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, iii. 7.}}}} '''unarmed''' (un-ärmd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unarmed'', ''onarmed'', ''unarmit''; < ''un-''1 + ''armed''.] '''1.''' Not having on arms or armor; not equipped with arms or weapons. {{smaller block|I am ''unarm’d''; forego this vantage, Greek.{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., v. 8. 9.}}}} '''2.''' Not furnished with scales, prickles, or other armature, as animals and plants; in ''entom.'', noting parts destitute of projections, spines, points, etc., where such structures are commonly found: as, ''unarmed'' tibiæ. '''unaspiring''' (un-as-pīr′ing), ''a.'' Not aspiring; not ambitious: as, a modest and ''unaspiring'' person. '''unassailable''' (un-a̤-sā′la̤-bl), ''a.'' Not assailable; incapable of being assailed; incontestable; hence, not to be moved or shaken from a purpose. {{smaller block|I do know but one That ''unassailable'' holds on his rank, Unshaked of motion.{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 1. 69.}}}} '''unassailed''' (un-a̤-sāld′), ''a.'' Not assailed; not attacked. {{smaller block|To keep my life and honour ''unassail’d.''{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 220.}}}} '''unassayed''' (un-a̤-sād′), ''a.'' Not essayed; not attempted; not subjected to assay or trial; untested. {{smaller block|To be ridd of these mortifying Propositions he leaves no tyrannical evasion ''unassaid.'' ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xi.}} '''unassimilated''' (un-a-sim′i-lā-ted), ''a.'' Not assimilated. {{smaller|(''a'') Not made to resemble; not brought into a relation of similarity. (''b'') In ''physiol.'', not united with and actually transformed into the fluid or solid constituents of the living body; not taken into the system as nutriment: as, food still ''unassimilated.''}} '''unassisted''' (un-a̤-sis′ted), ''a.'' Not assisted; not aided or helped; unaided. ''Addison.'' '''unassuetude''' (un-as′wẹ̄-tūd), ''n.'' Unaccustomedness. [Rare.] {{smaller block|We walked about for an hour or two, admiring the beauty and grand bearing of the women [of Genezzano], and the picturesque vivacity and ever-renewing ''unassuetude'' of the whole scene. {{right|''Lowell'', Fireside Travels, p. 252.}}}} '''unassuming''' (un-a̤-sū′ming), ''a.'' Not assuming; not bold or forward; not arrogant; modest; not forthputting; retiring. {{smaller block|Thou ''unassuming'' common-place Of Nature, with that homely face. {{right|''Wordsworth'', To the Same Flower (the Daisy).}}}} '''unassured''' (un-a̤-shörd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not assured; not bold or confident.—'''2†.''' Not to be trusted. {{smaller block|The fayned friends, the ''unassured'' foes. {{right|''Spenser'', Hymn in Honour of Love, l. 263.}}}} '''3.''' Not insured against loss: as, goods ''unassured.'' '''unattached''' (un-a̤-tacht′), ''a.'' Not attached; free. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In ''law'', not seized on account of debt. (''b'') ''Milit.'', not belonging to any special body of troops or to the staff, as an officer who is waiting orders.}} '''unattainable''' (un-a̤-tā′na̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be attained or gained. '''unattainableness''' (un-a̤-tā′na̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unattainable, or beyond reach. '''unattainted''' (un-a̤-tān′ted), ''a.'' Not attainted; not corrupted; not affected; hence, impartial. {{smaller block|With ''unattainted'' eye, Compare her face with some that I shall show. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 2. 90.}}}} '''unattempted''' (un-a̤-temp′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not attempted; not tried; not essayed; not undertaken. {{smaller block|Things ''unattempted'' yet in prose or rhyme. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 16.}}}}
